name: Battle of Adrianople

phases.title: The armies face each other below the hill
phases.text: The Goths held a wagon circle on a hilltop, and the Romans, tired and thirsty after a march, came up facing it. Both sides drew up in battle order, and the Gothic cavalry was away.
phases.when: About two in the afternoon, 9 August 378

phases.title: The shield-archers attack without orders
phases.text: Units of the imperial guard began the fight on their own and attacked the Goths without support. They were easily pushed back.

phases.title: The left wing reaches the wagons
phases.text: The shield-archers fell back while the Roman left wing pressed on until it reached the circle of wagons. By then, the accounts say, it was too late.

phases.title: The Gothic cavalry returns and surrounds the Romans
phases.text: The Gothic cavalry came back from foraging and arrived to support the infantry. It surrounded the Roman troops, who were already in disarray after the failed assault.

phases.title: The Romans are driven back and routed
phases.text: The Romans retreated to the base of the hill, where they could not manoeuvre in their heavy armour. Casualties and exhaustion led to a rout, and the cavalry kept up the attack until nightfall.

note: The precise location of the battle is uncertain, and the accounts do not say how the Roman army was drawn up beyond its left wing, so the rest of the Roman troops are drawn as one body facing the hill. The Romans marched north from Adrianople, so they are drawn at the foot of the field facing north, and the left wing stands on the west side. The shield-archers are drawn beside the main body because the accounts do not say where they stood. The Gothic infantry is drawn in front of the wagon circle, which the accounts say it defended; its exact place is not given. The Gothic cavalry is off the plan until it returns, and the accounts do not say from which side it came: it is drawn arriving from the west. Another account has the Roman left flank destroyed by the cavalry; the first account has the whole army retreating to the foot of the hill.
